claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys is primarily governed by the degree of aluminum-induced local chemical ordering.
Aluminum-induced local chemical ordering governs the balance of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
Increasing aluminum content relative to an equimolar baseline promotes formation of a B2-like ordered phase.
The B2-like ordered phase forms within a disordered matrix.
Aluminum lowers the free energy of the ordered state.
Competition between configurational entropy and ordering energy determines phase stability.
The equimolar baseline is predominantly disordered or only minimally ordered under standard processing conditions.
Equilibrium or near-equilibrium thermal processing allows chemical ordering to develop.
Higher aluminum concentration increases ordering energy.
The increase in ordering energy stabilizes a B2-type phase.
Competition between ordering and configurational entropy produces a two-phase microstructure.
The resulting two-phase microstructure can maintain high-temperature strength.
The resulting two-phase microstructure can maintain radiation resilience.
The resulting two-phase microstructure can preserve cryogenic toughness.
The aluminum-enriched alloy will have a larger B2 phase fraction or greater chemical short-range order than the baseline.
Greater B2 ordering will correlate with improved phase stability during high-temperature exposure.
Greater B2 ordering will correlate with improved phase stability during radiation exposure.
The aluminum-enriched alloy will preserve cryogenic toughness or suffer only a modest reduction.

contradictions.description: Increasing the aluminum atomic concentration while holding all four other elemental concentrations constant is not possible for a normalized alloy composition. The hypothesis does not state whether Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni are reduced proportionally or whether 'constant' refers to their ratios rather than their individual atomic percentages.
